opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a great question, and I think one of the first things to say is that we have a tendency to lump these things together, and it's very important to pull them apart. In humans and in other animals they come as a package. Consciousness, intelligence, creativity, the capacity for suffering, a sense of self: in us they all go together, so it's natural to assume they must always go together. But I don't think that's necessarily so. When we start thinking about AI, and especially about the very strange, exotic kinds of entities we're now building, we may find these things coming apart.

That said, I do think there's an interesting and deep relationship between at least some aspects of consciousness and cognition. I've long been sympathetic to global workspace theory, the idea from Bernard Baars and later Stanislas Dehaene and others. On that view, what's distinctive about conscious information processing is that it's broadcast across the whole brain. You have lots of specialist processes working in parallel, and when something becomes conscious, it's made available to all of them at once. Memory, planning, language, motor control can all bring their resources to bear on it.

If you take that seriously, the connection to intelligence and creativity becomes quite intuitive. Creativity is often about combining things in novel ways: bringing an idea from one domain into contact with resources from a completely different domain. A global workspace is exactly the kind of architecture that makes that possible. It lets the whole of your cognitive repertoire bear on a novel situation, rather than just running a routine, habitual response. So in the biological case there seems to be a functional link. Consciousness, in that sense, is part of what enables the flexible, general-purpose kind of intelligence we have.

But I'd be careful about two things. First, that functional story is about what's sometimes called access consciousness. It leaves open the harder questions about experience: whether there's something it's like, and whether something can suffer. Second, just because broadcast and integration are how biology achieved general intelligence, it doesn't follow that it's the only way to achieve it. Large language models show remarkable linguistic ability, and arguably some forms of creativity, yet it's far from obvious that they have anything like a global workspace in the relevant sense, let alone experience.

So my answer is that there's a real relationship in the case of humans and animals, and a good scientific story can be told about it. But when we move to the space of possible minds, what I've called conscious exotica, we should be open to finding intelligence without consciousness, or perhaps forms of consciousness quite unlike ours. And we should be very cautious about our language, because our everyday concepts were shaped around creatures like us.

r001.rationale: The response links global broadcast to flexible intelligence, but does not describe ordinary talk about awareness of the world as tied to behavioral capacities for dealing flexibly with it.

r002.rationale: It says consciousness and cognition may come apart, but does not frame this as asking when one concept would apply without the other.

r003.rationale: AlphaGo is not mentioned as an example.

r004.rationale: It says consciousness and cognitive abilities occur together in animals, but does not identify observable animal abilities as a proxy for attributing consciousness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that these things come apart, conceptually at least. It's very tempting to bundle them all together, because in the human case they all arrive as a package. We're conscious, we're intelligent, some of us are creative, and it all seems to come from the same place. But when you start thinking carefully about artificial systems, or indeed about non-human animals, you realise you have to pull them apart.

So intelligence, on one reading, is just the capacity to achieve goals in a wide range of environments, to solve problems, to generalise. And there's nothing in that definition that obviously requires there to be anything it is like to be the system doing it, to use Nagel's phrase. A chess engine is, in a narrow sense, very intelligent, and I don't think anybody wants to say there's something it's like to be Stockfish. Large language models push this much further. They exhibit a remarkable breadth of what you'd be inclined to call intelligent behaviour, and yet the question of whether there's any inner life there is, I'd say, completely open and in some ways confused.

Creativity is interesting because I think it's actually easier to attribute to a system than consciousness. If a system produces something novel and valuable that it wasn't explicitly programmed to produce, I'm fairly relaxed about calling that creative, in a functional sense. Again, that doesn't settle anything about experience.

Now, consciousness is where I get more careful, and I'd follow Wittgenstein here. The word doesn't pick out a single hidden thing that's either present or absent. It's a cluster. There's awareness of the world, there's self-awareness, there's the capacity for suffering and joy, there's the sense of being a continuing subject through time. In humans these are intertwined, but they can come apart. And crucially, our concepts for all of them are rooted in the way we use the words in relation to other embodied creatures that live in a shared world with us. When we meet something like a language model, which has no body, no persistent self, which is in some sense many characters at once, our ordinary concepts just don't straightforwardly apply. It's not that the answer is hidden from us. It's that we don't yet know what we would be asking.

So the short version is: intelligence and creativity are, I think, separable from consciousness and can be realised without it. But I'd add one caveat. In biological creatures, consciousness and cognition evolved together for good reasons. The integration of information, the modelling of the self in the world, attention, all of that does real cognitive work. So it's at least possible that certain kinds of very general, flexible intelligence, the kind that has to cope with an open-ended world through a single body over time, would end up with something consciousness-like whether you intended it or not. That's not a claim that current systems have it. It's just a reason not to be too confident about the separation holding at every level.

r003.rationale: It gives Stockfish as an example of intelligence without consciousness, but does not use AlphaGo.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish consciousness from intelligence and creativity, at least conceptually. Intelligence and creativity concern what a system can do: solve problems, adapt to new circumstances, produce something novel. With consciousness, we’re also asking whether there’s something it’s like to be that system—whether it has subjective experience. Those aren’t obviously the same question.

Now, in our own case, these things are closely intertwined. We consciously reflect on problems, imagine possibilities, and evaluate ideas. But a great deal of the processing that makes those activities possible isn’t conscious. An idea can simply occur to you without your having any access to how it was produced.

So I wouldn’t assume that increasingly intelligent or creative behaviour necessarily brings consciousness with it. Equally, I wouldn’t make sophisticated intelligence a prerequisite for experience. The interesting question is which mechanisms support these different capacities, and whether some of those mechanisms are shared. We need to investigate that relationship rather than build it into our definitions.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes consciousness as subjective experience from abilities such as solving problems and adapting, but does not describe ordinary talk about awareness of the world as linked to flexible behavior.

r002.rationale: It says consciousness and cognitive abilities need not coincide, but does not frame their dissociability in terms of when we would apply one concept without the other.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo as an example.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss animals’ observable cognitive abilities as a basis for attributing consciousness.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be quite careful to distinguish them. Intelligence and creativity are things we can investigate in terms of what a system can do: can it solve problems, adapt to new situations, produce something novel? Consciousness, in the sense of subjective experience, raises a different question: is there something it’s like to be that system?

Of course, these things are closely connected in our own case. When I’m working on a problem or having a creative thought, some of that activity is conscious. But a great deal of the processing that makes it possible isn’t accessible to me. An idea can just pop into your head, and you don’t know where it came from. So even in humans, we shouldn’t identify intelligence or creativity with conscious thought.

Then there’s the question of what consciousness contributes functionally. Perhaps making information available across many different cognitive processes helps us behave flexibly, reason about unfamiliar situations, and report what we’re thinking. We can study those capacities scientifically. But explaining those functions and explaining why there should be subjective experience are not obviously the same task.

So I’d resist assuming that a sufficiently intelligent or creative machine must therefore be conscious. Its abilities would give us something important to explain, but they wouldn’t, by themselves, settle the question of experience.
